section_summary: This section comprises diplomatic records, monthly political reports, lists of despatches and telegrams, and Division of Far Eastern Affairs memoranda from July through October 1932 concerning internal and foreign affairs of Japan. A primary focus is Japan's formal de jure recognition of Manchukuo through the Changchun Protocol and mounting tensions with the League of Nations over the findings of the Lytton Commission of Inquiry. Domestic political developments include the proceedings of the 63rd extraordinary session of the Diet convened for rural and agrarian relief, military influence over civilian politics, right-wing assassination conspiracies targeting cabinet ministers, and widespread public anti-American sentiment exacerbated by war psychology and espionage scares.

subfiles.about: A chronological list of despatches Nos. 34 through 74 transmitted by the American Embassy in Tokyo to the Department of State during July 1932.
keywords: League of Nations Commission of Inquiry
subfiles.summary: This document catalogs despatches Nos. 34 through 74 sent to the Department of State by the American Embassy in Tokyo during July 1932. Topics include internal unrest in Japan, political reaction to President Hoover's disarmament proposal, press censorship bans, and findings of the League of Nations Commission of Inquiry. It also records Ambassador Grew's addresses before various civic organizations, reports on Soviet-Japanese relations, and routine consular and embassy administrative business.
subfiles.title: Despatches Sent to the Department During July 1932

subfiles.about: A chronological list of telegrams Nos. 179 through 203 sent by the American Embassy in Tokyo to the Department of State during July 1932.
keywords: League of Nations Commission of Inquiry
subfiles.summary: This document lists telegrams Nos. 179 through 203 forwarded by the American Embassy in Tokyo to the Department of State during the month of July 1932. The telegrams report on diplomatic developments regarding Manchuria, including international representations over the Dairen customs, Japanese troop movements, and the impending recognition of Manchukuo. They also record the Tokyo arrival of the League of Nations Commission of Inquiry, Count Uchida's appointment as Foreign Minister, and routine embassy administrative transactions.
subfiles.title: Telegrams Sent to the Department During July 1932

subfiles.about: A newspaper report detailing Japanese War Minister Sadao Araki's interview with members of the League of Nations Commission of Inquiry concerning the establishment of Manchukuo.
keywords: League of Nations Commission of Inquiry
subfiles.summary: This newspaper clipping reports on a Tokyo interview between War Minister Lieutenant-General Sadao Araki and four visiting members of the League of Nations Commission of Inquiry (Count Aldrovandi, General McCoy, Dr. Schnee, and General Claudel). General Araki denied that Japan created Manchukuo, claiming that local Chinese established independence by taking advantage of Japan's self-defensive actions. He insisted that Manchuria and Mongolia represent Japan's vital lifeline, declared that Japanese recognition of Manchukuo would not violate the Nine Power Treaty, and firmly rejected Chinese suzerainty over the new state.
subfiles.title: Denies Japan Helped in Setting Up State: General Araki Tells League Commission Independence Was Inevitable

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum highlighting and analyzing newly reported information from the Tokyo Embassy's August 1932 monthly report on Japan.
subfiles.from: Laurence E. Salisbury, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: This memorandum by Laurence E. Salisbury in the Division of Far Eastern Affairs provides an analysis of Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 111 covering August 1932. It highlights Foreign Office spokesman Shiratori's deliberate attacks on Secretary Stimson's speech, patriotic backlash against Vice Admiral Nomura's proposed goodwill trip, and dissension within the Japanese Cabinet regarding the recognition of Manchukuo. The memorandum also summarizes military influence in domestic affairs, severe agrarian debt, Indian tariff increases on Japanese cotton textiles, an uncovered plot to assassinate Prime Minister Saito and other cabinet ministers, and a proposal to halve enrollment at private universities.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo's Monthly Report for August, 1932
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Division of Far Eastern Affairs

subfiles.about: American Embassy Tokyo Despatch No. 111 transmitting Report No. 71 on political, diplomatic, military, and economic conditions in Japan during August 1932.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 111 from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits Embassy Report No. 71 (prepared by S. Walter Washington) detailing Japanese affairs during August 1932. The report covers Japanese-American friction sparked by Foreign Office spokesman Shiratori's denunciations of Secretary Stimson's address, diplomatic preparations for recognizing Manchukuo, General Muto's mission as envoy and Kwantung Army commander, and the Russo-Japanese provisional fisheries treaty. Domestically, it examines the 63rd extraordinary session of the Diet convened for rural relief, agrarian distress, political party maneuvers, the Meiji Sugar tax evasion scandal, an uncovered reactionary assassination plot against Premier Saito and his colleagues, and financial strains related to the falling yen.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 111: Monthly Report on Conditions in Japan during the Month of August, 1932 (Report No. 71)

subfiles.about: A chronological list of despatches Nos. 75 through 110 sent by the American Embassy in Tokyo to the Department of State during August 1932.
subfiles.summary: This document lists despatches Nos. 75 through 110 transmitted by the American Embassy in Tokyo to the Department of State in August 1932. The listed despatches address significant diplomatic and military topics, such as extraordinary military preparations in Japan, Dr. Thomas Baty's legal opinion on recognizing Manchukuo, the League of Nations Commission of Inquiry, and emergency relief debates in the Diet. Other despatches cover Japanese fishing operations in Alaskan waters, trade agreements concerning French Indo-China, emigration to Brazil, and routine embassy administrative accounts.
subfiles.title: Despatches Sent to the Department During August 1932

subfiles.about: A chronological list of telegrams Nos. 204 through 222 forwarded by the American Embassy in Tokyo to the Department of State during August 1932.
subfiles.summary: This document catalogs telegrams Nos. 204 through 222 sent by the American Embassy in Tokyo to the Department of State during August 1932. The telegrams report on military developments in Jehol, General Muto's appointment to Manchuria, the reaction of the Japanese Foreign Office to Secretary Stimson's foreign policy address, and the formulation of a draft treaty with Manchukuo. They also record Count Uchida's foreign policy address in the Diet, domestic press bans, embassy staff assignments, and the appointment of Hiroshi Saito as Japanese Chargé d'Affaires in Washington.
subfiles.title: Telegrams Sent to the Department During August 1932

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum summarizing key points and observations from Tokyo's September 1932 monthly report on Japan.
subfiles.from: Laurence E. Salisbury, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: This memorandum prepared by Laurence E. Salisbury in the Division of Far Eastern Affairs reviews Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 145 covering conditions in Japan during September 1932. It highlights widespread popular anti-American sentiment and war psychology, the restrained international reaction to Japan's recognition of Manchukuo, and friction surrounding the status of the Kwantung Leased Territory and extraterritoriality. The memorandum also details official Japanese hostility toward the forthcoming Lytton Commission report, the weakening of the Minseito party following the death of Tasuku Egi, heavy withdrawals from postal savings accounts, and economic hurdles confronting an economic bloc between Japan and Manchuria.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo's Monthly Report for September, 1932
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Division of Far Eastern Affairs

subfiles.about: American Embassy Tokyo Despatch No. 145 transmitting Report No. 72 on political, international, legislative, and economic conditions in Japan during September 1932.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
keywords: National City Bank of New York
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 145 from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits Embassy Report No. 72 (drafted by S. Walter Washington) covering Japanese affairs during September 1932. The report examines anti-American espionage suspicions illustrated by the National City Bank incident in Osaka, the formal de jure recognition of Manchukuo through the Changchun Protocol signed September 15 by General Muto, and the arrival of Manchukuo envoy Pao Kuan-cheng in Tokyo. It also analyzes Japanese defiance toward the League of Nations upon delivery of the Lytton Commission report, the proceedings and legislative output of the 63rd extraordinary Diet session, political realignment among the Seiyukai and Kokumin Domei following Tasuku Egi's death, domestic economic trends, and a proposed Brazilian coffee concession.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 145: Monthly Report on Conditions in Japan during the Month of September, 1932 (Report No. 72)
